question: Does family practice at residency teaching sites reflect community practice?
answer: Residency teaching sites in northeast Ohio closely resembled national community family practice: 15 of the top 20 reason-for-visit codes and 14 of the top 20 diagnoses were identical to NAMCS data for FPs/GPs, and mean visit duration differed by only 1 minute. Some differences existed: residency sites saw slightly more children, women, Black patients, and Medicare/Medicaid patients, and offered more preventive and therapeutic services but fewer diagnostic services and consultations. A separate comparison found that, after controlling for patient mix, residents had longer visits, a less technical focus, and more time on health behavior change, prevention, and counseling than community family physicians.

question: Serovar specific immunity to Neisseria gonorrhoeae: does it exist?
answer: In a clinic study of 508 gonorrhoea episodes (22 patients with repeat infections), serovars isolated after a repeat infection did not differ significantly in prevalence from those without repeat infections, so no evidence of serovar-specific protective immunity was found. The site of the initial infection also did not appear to influence which serovar was isolated in the subsequent infection.

question: Immunohistochemical assessment of steroid hormone receptors in tissues of the anal canal. Implications for anal incontinence?
answer: Estrogen receptors were found in the smooth muscle of the internal anal sphincter in all females examined (10/10) and in the perimuscular connective tissue of all females (12/12), so the anal canal has the receptor prerequisite for a hormonal influence on continence. About 50% of ER-positive tissues in females were also PR-positive, whereas no specific ER or PR staining was seen in the striated muscle of the external sphincter in either sex. Only one of seven males showed PR staining (smooth muscle only), and ER was found in four of seven males, so receptor expression was more consistent in females.

question: Can nonproliferative breast disease and proliferative breast disease without atypia be distinguished by fine-needle aspiration cytology?
answer: In a review of 51 FNA smears with biopsy-proven diagnoses, only one cytologic feature (a swirling pattern of epithelial cells) differed significantly between proliferative breast disease without atypia and nonproliferative breast disease, so the two were not reliably distinguishable by FNA cytology. A swirling pattern was seen in 76% (13/17) of proliferative cases versus 35% (12/34) of nonproliferative cases (P = 0.008), meaning it overlaps considerably between the two groups.

question: Are endothelial cell patterns of astrocytomas indicative of grade?
answer: Endothelial/vascular patterns in astrocytomas differed by grade: normal-like vessel patterns in diffuse low-grade tumors, versus increased vessel density with glomeruloid clusters, intimal hyperplasia, loss of vessel wall integrity and numerous vWF-positive single cells/microvessels in intermediate-grade, anaplastic astrocytoma and glioblastoma. question: Is a mandatory general surgery rotation necessary in the surgical clerkship?
answer: In a study of 54 students who chose any two surgical rotations, clerkships with and without general surgery showed no differences in written exam, OSCE, ward evaluation, self-assessment, or satisfaction scores, and no concerns related to the absence of general surgery were identified. Across four teaching hospitals with markedly varying clinical experience, postrotation scores were similar, suggesting that specific clinical exposures are not strictly required for comparable examination performance.

question: Is laparoscopic sonography a reliable and sensitive procedure for staging colorectal cancer?
answer: In 33 colorectal cancer patients, laparoscopic ultrasonography (LUS) was highly sensitive for staging: 100% for hepatic metastases and 94% for nodal metastases, versus 62.5% and 18% for preoperative staging and 75% and 6% for laparoscopy. LUS changed the planned therapeutic approach in 4 patients (12%) on its own. Laparoscopy plus LUS together changed the approach in 11 patients (33%).

question: Is there a role for leukocyte and CRP measurements in the diagnosis of acute appendicitis in the elderly?
answer: In 83 elderly patients operated on for suspected appendicitis, mean leukocyte count and CRP did not differ significantly between those with and without appendicitis. However, none of the 73 patients with acute appendicitis had both values unelevated, so normal values on both tests argue against appendicitis and the tests have a role as a combined rule-out aid.

question: Can medical students contribute to quality assurance programmes in day surgery?
answer: Final-year medical students followed 621 day surgery cases (14.1% of cases sampled) and contributed to quality assurance by identifying problems such as inappropriate patient and procedure selection, inadequate pain management, and discharge, communication and resource issues. Students also made concrete recommendations, including multilingual videotapes and patient information sheets for non-English speaking patients, avoiding bilateral surgical procedures, and improved links with local medical officers, and they developed new guidelines and protocols. In a separate (non-day-surgery) setting, student groups in a paediatric clerkship identified, analysed and presented medication errors and patient safety concerns, suggesting students can take part in safety and quality analysis more generally.

answer: Variation in carotid endarterectomy use was not explained by population need: across English districts, utilisation varied 14-fold, with no association with district stroke mortality (r=-0.06) or stroke admission rates (r=0.17). question: Clinician assessment for acute chest syndrome in febrile patients with sickle cell disease: is it accurate enough?
answer: Clinician assessment was not accurate enough: in a prospective study of febrile SCD patients, physician sensitivity for predicting ACS was only 39%, and 61% (14/23) of CXR-confirmed ACS cases were not clinically suspected before the radiograph. Symptoms and examination did not reliably identify ACS: apart from splinting (17% vs 0%), no symptom or physical finding distinguished patients with ACS, and 57% of ACS patients had completely normal physical examinations. Accuracy did not improve significantly with more pediatric training, and unsuspected ACS had the same course (hospital stay, oxygen use, transfusion need) as detected ACS, so missed cases were not milder.

question: Is delayed gastric emptying following pancreaticoduodenectomy related to pylorus preservation?
answer: The evidence is mixed: one retrospective comparison found delayed gastric emptying more common after pylorus-preserving Whipple than standard Whipple (61% vs 41%), while another found no significant difference between pylorus preservation and polar inferior gastrectomy (20% vs 35%, p = 0.88). question: Risk stratification in emergency surgical patients: is the APACHE II score a reliable marker of physiological impairment?

answer: In an Italian primary care study, only 27.6% of PUD patients (596 of 2162) received H. pylori eradication therapy, which is antibiotic-based, and the rate was 37.7% even among those with a definitive diagnosis. question: Does ultrasound imaging before puncture facilitate internal jugular vein cannulation?
answer: In a randomized trial of 240 patients, prepuncture ultrasound did not improve internal jugular cannulation when respiratory jugular venodilation was identifiable (first-attempt access 85.7% vs 83.5%; success 95.6% vs 96.9%). question: Should tumor depth be included in prognostication of soft tissue sarcoma?
answer: In a population-based series of 490 adults with extremity or trunk wall soft tissue sarcoma, multivariate analysis showed no major prognostic effect of tumor depth once grade and size were accounted for. In a separate series of extremity sarcomas treated with limb-sparing surgery and radiation, only tumor size significantly influenced distant metastasis and survival; depth was not among the covariates analyzed.

question: Do microbiological factors account for poor pregnancy outcome among unmarried pregnant women in Poland?

question: Is fear of anaphylactic shock discouraging surgeons from more widely adopting percutaneous and laparoscopic techniques in the treatment of liver hydatid cyst?
answer: In a survey of 30 surgeons in northern Jordan, fear of anaphylaxis and/or dissemination was the main reason given by 21 of 27 surgeons (78%) who did not use percutaneous or laparoscopic treatment for liver hydatid cysts. Only 3 of the 30 surgeons (10%) considered laparoscopy as first-line treatment, indicating low adoption of minimal-access techniques. Experimental work suggests that spillage risk can be reduced with proper laparoscopic technique, such as aspiration through a large cannula under vacuum or a cannula sealed to the liver with glue, whereas simple needle aspiration failed to prevent spillage.

question: Ovarian torsion in children: is oophorectomy necessary?
answer: Oophorectomy does not appear to be necessary for ovarian torsion in children: in one pediatric series, 17 of 36 torsions were treated by detorsion with or without cystectomy, and follow-up sonogram or biopsy in 14 of those 17 showed a normal ovary with follicular development in every case. question: Can we rely on arterial line sampling in performing activated plasma thromboplastin time after cardiac surgery?
answer: Arterial line sampling cannot be relied on for APTT after cardiac surgery: in 49 patients the median arterial APTT ratio was significantly higher than the simultaneous peripheral venous value (1.32 vs 1.1, P<0.001). Heparin contamination of arterial samples was supported by thromboelastography, where the R-value was longer without heparinase (about 406 s) than with heparinase (about 318 s, P<0.05). INR values were statistically similar by both routes. A survey of 22 UK cardiothoracic ICUs found that heparinized arterial lines were by far the most common port used to draw blood for APTT ratio, so the contamination problem relates to routine practice. In vitro work in healthy volunteers is consistent with heparin interfering with some coagulation tests, though this study did not examine APTT specifically.

question: Does screening or surveillance for primary hepatocellular carcinoma with ultrasonography improve the prognosis of patients?
answer: In a study of 680 HCC cases, ultrasonographic screening was associated with significantly better prognosis: adjusted odds ratios for screened vs unscreened were about 0.33-0.37 for 1-, 2-, and 3-year survival outcomes, and surveillance vs nonsurveillance gave odds ratios of 0.44-0.58. question: Does parity increase insulin resistance during pregnancy?
answer: In 1880 pregnant women, higher parity was associated with lower insulin sensitivity and higher C-peptide/glucose in univariate analysis, but these relationships were no longer significant after adjustment for age, pregestational BMI and weight gain. question: Does rural or urban residence make a difference to neonatal outcome in premature birth?
answer: Rural residence was associated with worse outcomes for very premature infants (<32 weeks) in NSW/ACT, with higher case-mix adjusted mortality (adjusted OR 1.26, 95% CI 1.07 to 1.48, p = 0.005) compared with urban residence. question: Is there any interest to perform ultrasonography in boys with undescended testis?

question: Is Panton-Valentine leucocidin associated with the pathogenesis of Staphylococcus aureus bacteraemia in the UK?
answer: Among 244 consecutive S. aureus bacteraemia isolates from 25 UK and Irish centres in 2005, only 4 (1.6%) carried PVL genes, all MSSA, suggesting PVL is rarely involved in bacteraemia pathogenesis in this setting. question: Is double-balloon enteroscopy an accurate method to diagnose small-bowel disorders?
answer: In a series of 44 patients with varied small-bowel indications, double-balloon enteroscopy (DBE) reached a diagnosis in 75% (33/44), with a therapeutic yield of 63.6% and only minor complications (sore throat in 9.1%). In a series of 66 patients, DBE endoscopically confirmed 74.4% of the abnormal findings from prior video-capsule endoscopy and found lesions that the capsule had missed in 3 cases. It also enabled therapy (electrocautery, biopsy, stricture dilation). In emergency DBE for overt obscure GI bleeding, a lesion amenable to hemostasis was found in 23 of 27 patients and 21 of those were treated successfully (77.8%). Dieulafoy's lesions were detected far more often with emergency DBE than with later DBE (40.7% vs 0.9%). A related single-balloon enteroscopy series (70 patients) found diagnoses in most patients but had a negative exam in 23/70, which suggests that balloon-assisted enteroscopy does not diagnose every case.

question: Are there gender differences in the reasons why African Americans delay in seeking medical help for symptoms of an acute myocardial infarction?
answer: In a cross-sectional study of 61 African American AMI patients, the factors associated with prehospital delay differed by gender, although the overall median delay was not significantly different (4.4 hours for women vs 3.5 hours for men). question: Systematic use of patient-rated depression severity monitoring: is it helpful and feasible in clinical psychiatry?
answer: Introducing the PHQ-9 for systematic depression severity monitoring was feasible and helpful in 19 diverse psychiatric practices: all 17 practices that completed the one-year project adopted it as a routine part of depression care. question: Does peritoneal dialysis affect halitosis in patients with end-stage renal disease?
answer: In 42 ESRD patients, halitosis scores were lower after 3 months of peritoneal dialysis than before it (2.39 ± 0.60 vs 3.90 ± 0.37), so PD therapy was associated with reduced halitosis. question: Should temperature be monitorized during kidney allograft preservation?
answer: Continuous temperature monitoring during kidney graft preservation revealed that actual temperatures differ between storage devices: the new Biotainer can stayed below 5°C for 57 hours, whereas the former can reached 5°C after about 10 hours 40 minutes. Monitoring was feasible with a probe recording every 10 minutes for four days; probe position within the transport pack did not change readings, and similar results were seen in actual human kidney grafts. Monitoring also showed that using 2 versus 4 kg of crushed ice gave similar temperature levels, which informs practical preservation procedures.

question: Identification of racial disparities in breast cancer mortality: does scale matter?

question: Does lung ischemia and reperfusion have an impact on coronary flow?
answer: In a swine model, 60 min of left lung ischemia followed by 60 min of reperfusion significantly reduced total coronary flow from baseline, with the lowest value at 60 min of reperfusion (-37.1%, p<0.003). question: Health care for immigrants in Europe: is there still consensus among country experts about principles of good practice?
answer: A three-round Delphi study of 134 experts in 16 EU Member States found a broad European consensus on most factors characterising good practice in health care for migrants, aggregated into 9 themes. question: Can fractional lasers enhance transdermal absorption of topical lidocaine in an in vivo animal model?
answer: In a pig model, Er:YAG fractional laser pretreatment enabled systemic absorption of topical 4% lidocaine: lidocaine and its metabolite MEGX were undetectable in serum from untreated skin but detectable after laser treatment. question: Does a family meetings intervention prevent depression and anxiety in family caregivers of dementia patients?

question: Mitral replacement or repair for functional mitral regurgitation in dilated and ischemic cardiomyopathy: is it really the same?
answer: In a study of 132 patients with functional MR and systolic dysfunction, repair and replacement were not equivalent: hospital mortality was 2.3% for repair versus 12.5% for replacement, and 2.5-year survival was 92% versus 73%. question: Internal derangement of the temporomandibular joint: is there still a place for ultrasound?
answer: In a study of 40 patients and 20 volunteers (120 TMJs) using MRI as the reference, static and dynamic high-resolution ultrasound had considerably lower sensitivity than MRI for detecting internal derangement, so it does not appear to hold a strong diagnostic place. Technical difficulties arose because surrounding bone structures limited ultrasound access to the joint.

question: Is human cytomegalovirus infection associated with hypertension?

question: Do European people with type 1 diabetes consume a high atherogenic diet?

question: Follow-up of patients with new cardiovascular implantable electronic devices: are experts' recommendations implemented in routine clinical practice?
answer: In a Medicare cohort of new CIED recipients, only 42.4% of eligible patients had the recommended in-person follow-up within 2 to 12 weeks, so expert recommendations were not routinely implemented for most patients. Adherence improved over time: 2-12 week follow-up rose from 40.3% in 2005 to 55.1% in 2009, and 0-16 week follow-up rose from 62.3% to 79.6%. Overall, 65.1% had a visit within 0-16 weeks and 78.0% had at least one in-person visit within 1 year, so a substantial minority had no timely follow-up. Adherence varied by race: 43.0% of white patients, 36.8% of black patients and 40.5% of patients of other races had follow-up within 2-12 weeks. In an ICD registry linked to Medicare claims, 30,256 patients received follow-up within 2-12 weeks versus 43,060 who did not, indicating that most patients did not receive the recommended visit during 2005-2008.

question: CPAP therapy in patients with idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis and obstructive sleep apnea: does it offer a better quality of life and sleep?

question: Attenuation of ischemia/reperfusion-induced ovarian damage in rats: does edaravone offer protection?

question: Treatment as prevention in resource-limited settings: is it feasible to maintain HIV viral load suppression over time?

question: Is trabecular bone related to primary stability of miniscrews?

question: Are there mental health differences between francophone and non-francophone populations in manitoba?

question: Can mass drug administration lead to the sustainable control of schistosomiasis?
answer: In Northern Samar, Philippines, schistosomiasis remained highly prevalent (27.1%) after more than 30 years of control efforts including MDA in the previous 5 years, so MDA did not achieve sustainable control there. question: Do parents recall and understand children's weight status information after BMI screening?

question: Nutritional assessment of gluten-free diet. Is gluten-free diet deficient in some nutrient?

question: Maternal creatine homeostasis is altered during gestation in the spiny mouse: is this a metabolic adaptation to pregnancy?

answer: In Annals of Emergency Medicine, reviewers whose work was cited gave a slightly higher mean desirability score (2.8 vs 2.5), but this difference disappeared after accounting for manuscript quality. question: Does septoplasty change the dimensions of compensatory hypertrophy of the middle turbinate?
answer: Radiological measurements taken before and at least one year after septoplasty showed no significant change in the bony or mucosal dimensions of the middle turbinate, on either the concave or convex side of the septum. question: Digital Tomosynthesis: A Viable Alternative to Noncontrast Computed Tomography for the Follow-Up of Nephrolithiasis?
answer: In a retrospective comparison of digital tomosynthesis (DT) with noncontrast CT in nephrolithiasis follow-up, DT showed similar stone detection rates to NCCT for stone count and stone area (mean area difference 16.5 mm2, p = 0.121). question: Gynecological cancer alarm symptoms: is contact with specialist care associated with lifestyle and socioeconomic status?
answer: In a Danish nationwide cohort of women reporting gynecological cancer alarm symptoms to their GP, higher educational level (a socioeconomic marker) was significantly associated with greater odds of specialist contact (OR 1.86, 95% CI 1.17-2.95). question: Is routine dissection of the station 9 lymph nodes really necessary for primary lung cancer?
answer: Routine station 9 lymph node dissection appears unnecessary: in a retrospective series of 1397 patients, station 9 metastasis occurred in only 3.45%, significantly lower than other mediastinal stations. question: Are performance measurement systems useful?
answer: A survey of 97 Italian healthcare managers found that strategic use of performance measurement systems directly and significantly (p<0.001) improved care processes. English NHS patient survey leads viewed the national patient survey results positively and reported widely using them in action planning, and they thought the results supported patient-centredness. question: Resection of colorectal liver metastases after second-line chemotherapy: is it worthwhile?
answer: Resection of colorectal liver metastases after two or more chemotherapy lines yielded meaningful survival: in 60 patients, 3-year and 5-year overall survival were 41% and 22%, with 3% postoperative mortality. In a large prospective cohort, overall survival from CLM diagnosis after two preoperative chemotherapy lines (n=791) did not differ from that after one line (n=5624): 5-year OS was 49% in both groups, with median OS 58.6 vs 58.9 months. Disease-free survival after hepatectomy was shorter after second-line chemotherapy than after first-line (median 17.2 vs 19.4 months; 5-year 15% vs 23%). Worse outcomes after second-line chemotherapy were linked to synchronous disease, minor pathologic response, positive primary nodes, extrahepatic disease, tumour progression on second line, and R2 resection, which can help identify patients less likely to benefit.

question: Visceral adipose tissue area measurement at a single level: can it represent visceral adipose tissue volume?
answer: A single-slice CT measurement of VAT area can reflect VAT volume when taken at the right level: the area at a slice 3 cm above the lower margin of L3 correlated most strongly with VAT volume (r = 0.853).

claims.text: A single-slice CT measurement of VAT area can reflect VAT volume when taken at the right level: the area at a slice 3 cm above the lower margin of L3 correlated most strongly with VAT volume (r = 0.853).

limitations.text: The study was small (30 men, 60 CT scans) and included only males who had workplace screenings, so the findings may not generalize to women or other populations.

The correlation with volume (r = 0.853) is strong but not perfect, and the result depends on choosing the optimal slice level. Other levels may represent volume less well, and no replication is reported.
